Fair Market Value: Purchase, Lease, and Asset Recovery on Disposal

Unit 2: Procurement, Contracts, and the Asset Lifecycle. Lesson 11 of 60 in CHTM Academy.

Two decisions bracket a device's life and both come to you for a number. At the front, finance asks whether to buy it or lease it. At the end, a vendor offers a trade-in credit on the replacement, and a used-equipment dealer offers cash. Somebody has to say what the old device is actually worth, and what has to happen to it before it leaves the building.

Fair market value, and what it is not

Fair market value is what a willing buyer would pay a willing seller today, with neither under pressure. It is not book value, which is an accounting position, and it is not replacement cost, which is what a new one costs. It is established from current market evidence: completed sales of the same model, dealer and broker quotes, auction results, and a professional appraisal where the value justifies one. Hospital policy should say who determines fair market value and who may accept an offer, because the manager who negotiates the replacement should not also be the sole judge of the trade-in credit.

Purchase, lease, and rental

Choice     Money it uses       What the hospital holds     What to read in the terms
Purchase   capital             the asset and every         nothing; the cost is yours
                               downstream cost             for the life
Capital    behaves like a      the asset in substance,     who maintains and insures
lease      purchase, paid      ending in ownership or a    it, the end-of-term buyout
           over a term         bargain purchase
Operating  operating money     use of the device for a     who maintains and insures
lease      across the term     term, then it goes back     it, return condition,
                                                           escalation, and renewal
Rental     operating money,    use for weeks or months     daily or monthly rate, who
           short term                                      services it, delivery

A capital lease is a purchase in substance, so the asset and the obligation land on the balance sheet. An operating lease spreads cost as an expense and leaves the device the lessor's property. Finance picks the structure; HTM's job is to say who services it, who insures it, what condition it must be returned in, whether the hospital may service it at all, and what happens to data on it at the end of term.

Asset recovery on disposal

Order of preference, highest value first: redistribute inside the organization or to a simulation or training center, then sell, then donate, then recycle.

  • Trade-in is convenient and usually the lowest value available. Price the open market before accepting it.
  • Resale through used-equipment companies and broker sites will draw bids. After the labor to list, negotiate, and load, it is often close to break-even, so count the labor.
  • Donation can put a device to work abroad. Policy must say who selects the charity and who may donate instead of sell, and the device must still be serviceable where it lands.
  • Recycling is the floor, and it is still a documented, compliant route rather than the loading dock.

One financial warning: disposing of an asset that is still being depreciated writes off its remaining book value, so finance agrees before the device moves.

The disposal process

  1. Approval under the hospital's policy, with finance notified of the book value.
  2. Data wiping or media destruction on anything that stored patient information. Selling or donating a device holding PHI is a HIPAA violation, and often only HTM knows the data is in there.
  3. Decontamination to the infection prevention standard, documented, before anyone handles it.
  4. Environmental handling for batteries, mercury, sealed sources, refrigerants, and electronics, which follow environmental rules rather than the dumpster.
  5. Documentation and inventory removal: a disposal record naming the asset, the method, the date, the wipe, and the signature, then the asset closed out of the CMMS and the ledger.
Exam tip: fair market value is today's market price, not book value and not replacement cost. A capital lease behaves like a purchase; an operating lease is an expense. Wipe the data and decontaminate before anything leaves, document the disposal, and get finance's agreement on remaining book value first.
Remember
Fair market value is what the market would pay today rather than book value, and every disposal runs approval, data wiping, decontamination, environmental handling, documentation, and removal from the inventory.
Deeper explanation

Fair Market Value: Purchase, Lease, and Asset Recovery on Disposal, explained slowly

Establishing fair market value on a real asset

A seven-year-old imaging system, original cost $400,000, ten-year useful life, no salvage.

Measure                    Value      What it is
Original cost            400,000      what the hospital paid
Accumulated depreciation 280,000      7 years x $40,000
Book value               120,000      cost minus accumulated depreciation
Replacement cost         520,000      what a new equivalent costs today
Dealer quotes, cash       38,000      two used-equipment dealers, as-is
Broker estimate, after    44,000      net of commission and de-installation
sale
Vendor trade-in credit    25,000      offered against the replacement
Fair market value         38,000      what a willing buyer pays today, from
to 44,000                             current market evidence

Four numbers, and only one of them is fair market value. The trade-in credit is $13,000 to $19,000 below the market, which is the usual relationship, and it is offered because it is convenient. Price the open market before you accept one, and have the hospital's policy name who determines fair market value so the person negotiating the replacement is not also the only judge of the old asset's worth.

Now the financial consequence. Selling for $40,000 against a $120,000 book value writes off $80,000 of remaining book value, and finance must agree to that in advance. Waiting three years until the asset is fully depreciated removes the write-off entirely, which is occasionally a real argument for timing a replacement.

The row in capitals is the one HTM exists to catch. A leased device returned at end of term with patient data still on its drive is a breach, and the lessor is not going to raise it.

The disposal record

Field                        Example entry
Asset number                 BM-14027
Manufacturer, model, serial  as recorded in the inventory
Reason for disposal          end of support; replaced under capital plan
Approval                     policy reference, approver name, date
Book value at disposal       $120,000, write-off agreed by finance, date
Data held                    yes: patient images on internal drive
Wipe or destruction method   drive removed and destroyed; certificate attached
Decontamination              performed, method, date, by whom
Environmental handling       lead shielding and batteries to the licensed route
Method of disposal           sold to dealer, $40,000, invoice reference
Date removed from inventory  with the CMMS record closed, not deleted
Signature                    manager, and the second signature policy requires

The CMMS record is closed rather than deleted, because a recall notice or an audit may still name that serial number next year.

What to memorize

Fair market value    what a willing buyer pays today; not book value, not
                     replacement cost
Capital lease        behaves like a purchase; the asset is on the balance sheet
Operating lease      an expense across the term; the device goes back
Order of preference  redistribute, sell, donate, recycle
Before it leaves     approval, data wipe, decontamination, environmental
                     handling, documentation, inventory removal
Financial check      remaining book value is written off; finance agrees first
